extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners and attorneys subject to USPTO disciplinary rules (and counsel handling reciprocal-discipline matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO applies when imposing reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24, including grounds to avoid identical discipline, standards for nunc pro tunc treatment, and related notification/administrative requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford / 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) standard for reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will impose identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence, and the Director finds a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) the imposition of the same discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal discipline proceedings are not de novo; a state disbarment creates a federal presumption that identical discipline is proper (Selling). The practitioner bears the burden to show, by clear and convincing evidence, a genuine issue of material fact on one of these grounds. Federal review is narrow and not a vehicle to retry the underlying disciplinary proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process requirement in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner. In disciplinary proceedings, due process is satisfied where a respondent received reasonable notice of the charges, attended and actively participated in hearings, was afforded opportunity to present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, and present argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples cited: Mathews v. Eldridge; In re Ruffalo; In re Squire; In re Zdravkovich. Mere disagreement with evidentiary rulings or legal conclusions by state tribunals is not, by itself, a deprivation of due process. The USPTO looks for factual showing of lack of notice/opportunity or other fundamental deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing that there was such infirmity of proof establishing the misconduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high, narrow standard—practitioner must show proof so lacking that the Office cannot accept the state tribunal's conclusion. Courts/USPTO afford state findings high respect; infirmity claims require clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that imposition of the same public discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence that applying identical discipline would produce a grave injustice. This is one of the limited Selling/§11.24(d)(1) defenses and is narrowly construed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and quantum of proof to avoid reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent/practitioner must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the Selling/§11.24(d)(1) elements to prevent imposition of identical discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple circuit decisions cited (e.g., In re Kramer, In re Friedman) establish this allocation and standard. The USPTO will not act as a court of review to discover garden-variety errors; the burden is strict and narrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline is not de novo (deference to state findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal disciplinary proceedings are not de novo proceedings; the Office accords a high degree of respect to the state tribunal's substantive findings and will not retry the original disciplinary proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will not re-litigate evidentiary rulings, judgment calls, or legal disagreements; only narrow Selling/§11.24(d)(1) showings can overcome the presumption in favor of identical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nunc pro tunc (concurrent) reciprocal discipline requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be imposed nunc pro tunc (contemporaneous with the state suspension) only if the practitioner promptly notified the OED Director of the suspension in the other jurisdiction and establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner voluntarily ceased all activities related to practice before the Office and complied with all provisions of § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary cessation of practice alone is insufficient; practitioner must show prompt notice to OED and compliance with the specific duties set out in §11.58. Failure to satisfy these requirements has led the USPTO to refuse nunc pro tunc treatment in prior matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of disciplined practitioners under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplined practitioners must comply with duties in §11.58, which include, among other things, filing notices of withdrawal in each patent and trademark application pending before the USPTO and providing notices of the discipline to all State and Federal jurisdictions and to all clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with §11.58 is a prerequisite for nunc pro tunc reciprocal discipline under §11.24(f). The practitioner bears the burden of proving §11.58 compliance by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO's available identical sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification imposed by the state, unless one of the Selling/§11.24(d)(1) defenses is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office's action mirrors the state sanction unless the practitioner meets the narrow burden to show a Selling element by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Director's discretion to publish notice and notify jurisdictions (37 C.F.R. § 11.59)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall give notice of public discipline and the reasons for the discipline to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the state(s) where the respondent is admitted, to courts where the respondent is known to be admitted, and to the public; and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the prescribed content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director retains discretion over the content of the public notice. The Final Order directs publication materially consistent with specified language and requires notification to other agencies and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequential administrative orders following discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical administrative consequences include: requiring the respondent to comply with §11.58 duties; dissociating the respondent's name from any Customer Numbers and USPTO verified electronic system accounts; prohibiting the respondent from applying for or obtaining a USPTO Customer Number or having his name added to a Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are routine administrative steps the Office may order in conjunction with reciprocal discipline to effectuate the suspension and protect USPTO processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 60(b)(2) standard (elements for vacating a judgment) as referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: To vacate a judgment under Rule 60(b)(2) based on newly discovered evidence, the movant must show: (1) the evidence was newly discovered since the final judgment or order; (2) due diligence to discover the new evidence; (3) the evidence is not merely cumulative or impeaching; (4) the evidence is material; and (5) the evidence is such that a new trial or reconsideration would probably produce a new result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites the district court's finding that the respondent failed to meet all five elements and therefore the Amended Motion to Vacate was legally frivolous. This Rule-60 standard was used to assess underlying litigation conduct and is cited as context for the state tribunal's findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and timing to seek judicial review of USPTO Director's final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of the final decision by the USPTO Director may be had by a petition filed with the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local rules (E.D. Va.) govern practice for bringing such petitions; this is the statutory avenue and timing for judicial review of the Director's order.
